analysis.one_liner: Bars meatpacking giants from owning, feeding, or controlling the livestock they slaughter.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support in 2007, the bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the 1921 Packers and Stockyards Act to make it illegal for large meatpacking companies to own, feed, or take operational control of livestock destined for their own slaughterhouses, restoring a separation between the companies that raise livestock and the companies that buy and slaughter it. Farmer-owned cooperatives, very small packers, and short-term purchases made within seven days of slaughter are exempt. The bill never got past the committee stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent livestock producers — family farms and ranches that raise cattle, hogs, and other animals for sale. With packers barred from raising their own supply, slaughterhouses would have to bid on the open market against each other, giving sellers more buyers and better price competition. Rural communities that depend on farm income would also gain, since contract arrangements that shift risk onto producers would be curtailed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits packers from owning, feeding, or controlling livestock through subsidiaries or arrangements that give the packer operational, managerial, or supervisory control so extensive that the producer no longer materially manages the operation [S3, S2].
It gives packers of cattle and other livestock 180 days to comply, and pork packers 18 months, so producers and packers have time to unwind existing captive arrangements [S3].
It preserves farmer-owned cooperatives, allowing them to keep owning and feeding livestock if a majority of ownership is held by active members who supply the animals for slaughter [S3, S2].

analysis.who_pays: The large meatpacking companies that own slaughterhouses and the industrial-scale livestock operations they control. Firms would have to give up vertically integrated supply chains, buy more animals on the open market, and accept thinner margins or greater price volatility. The added competition could put some upward pressure on wholesale meat prices, which consumers would ultimately see at the store.

drawbacks.text: The exemptions are broad enough to worry even supporters of the principle: packers may buy livestock within seven days of slaughter, and any packer with only one processing plant, or one not required to report prices daily, is fully exempt [S3, S2]. A packer could structure most of its supply through the seven-day window or through single-plant subsidiaries, limiting the rule's real effect.

The industry argues that packer-owned livestock improves efficiency, quality control, and consistency for consumers, and that forcing divestiture could raise costs in a thin-margin business; independent economists have long debated how much captive supply actually depresses farmer prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core fix is aimed at a real problem — a handful of packing firms both buy and raise livestock, which can crowd out independent sellers — but the carve-outs for the seven-day window and single-plant packers leave room for the practice to continue in new forms. Weighing the competition benefits to farmers against possible wholesale price effects and enforcement complexity, this is a well-intended bill whose main risk is being written so as to be avoidable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it sat without a hearing or a vote until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Grassley introduced the bill on January 16, 2007, joined by Senators Dorgan, Enzi, and Harkin [S3, S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
That referral was the bill's last action of record; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred in the 110th Congress [S5].
Seven senators cosponsored the bill — six Democrats and one Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies benefit: the vertical integration between packing and livestock production that the bill targeted remained untouched, and independent producers gained no new bidding leverage. The 110th Congress's failure to act preserved the status quo for packers with no offsetting action on the issue.

against.name: Large meatpacking companies
against.role: Beef and pork packers with integrated livestock operations
against.what_they_did: Opposed a packer ownership ban, which threatened to end their practice of owning or contracting livestock through their own feeding operations.

sides.party_line_note: The bill crossed party lines from the start: a Republican sponsor (Grassley) joined by three Democratic and one additional Republican original cosponsor, with final cosponsorship of 6 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].

industries.note: The bill would force the biggest packers to stop owning, feeding, or operationally controlling the livestock they slaughter, ending captive supply arrangements. Independent producers would face more open-market bidding; consumers could face some wholesale price pressure.
The bill explicitly exempts cooperatives whose majority ownership is held by active member-producers, letting them keep integrating raising and slaughter while big packers cannot.
Packers with one processing plant, or ones not required to report prices daily, are exempt from the ban, giving them a competitive advantage over the largest integrated firms.

industries.industry: Industrial livestock feeding operations owned by packers
industries.note: These feeding operations — often packer subsidiaries — would have to be divested or restructured within the transition period (18 months for swine, up to 180 days for other livestock).
